summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to inspect welding and fabrication work. You will learn to plan an inspection from the drawings, specification and ITP, check the records behind the welds, inspect welds by eye and with gauges, measure fabrications and bolted connections, carry out dye penetrant and magnetic particle tests, understand ultrasonic and radiographic results, judge destructive tests, and write clear reports, release notes and non-conformance reports while staying independent.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **welding and fabrication inspection**: planning an inspection from the drawings and specification, checking documents and materials, visual and dimensional inspection, inspecting bolted connections, carrying out dye penetrant and magnetic particle tests, understanding ultrasonic and radiographic results, judging destructive tests, and recording and reporting what you find, including non-conformances.

An inspector's signature says that work meets its requirements. To give it honestly you must know what the requirement is, measure the work accurately, judge it against the written limits, and record it so that someone who was not there can see exactly what was checked.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, welders and leading hands who inspect their own and others' work, and staff moving into quality control in fabrication shops.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Plan the inspection
Collect the drawings, specification, code limits and inspection and test plan; decide what to check, when, with which tools.
Review the records
Check WPSs, welder qualifications, material and consumable certificates against the work.
Inspect welds by eye and with gauges
Check size, profile and surface defects; measure undercut, cap height, misalignment and fillet throats; judge them against the limits.
Inspect fabrications dimensionally
Measure lengths, camber, sweep, twist, flatness, squareness and hole positions from datums.
Inspect bolted connections
Check bolt grade, length, washers, holes and tightness by the specified method.
Carry out surface NDT
Do colour-contrast dye penetrant and magnetic particle tests to a written method.
Use volumetric NDT results
Understand ultrasonic and radiographic testing and their reports, and choose the right test for a job.
Judge destructive tests
Prepare and judge macro sections, fillet break, nick-break and bend tests.
Record and report
Write clear inspection reports, release notes and non-conformance reports; stay independent.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on the inspector's role, planning, visual and dimensional inspection, gauges, acceptance limits, PT, MT, UT, RT, destructive tests, bolted connections, reporting and safety, with some sums.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (for example developer, dwell time, probe, IQI, yoke, fusion line, edge distance, macro, indication, calibration block) and essays in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: dye penetrant and magnetic particle testing of welded test pieces with inspection reports; and dimensional and bolted-connection inspection of a fabricated beam or frame, ending in a release note or NCR.

blocks.note: The limits in this kit's examples are "for this job". Real limits come from the code, specification or drawing the job uses. In the exam and at work, always judge against the limit you are given, not a figure you remember.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: The inspector's role, planning and records review

blocks.p: The inspector judges work against **written requirements**: the drawing, the specification and the code. Your job is not to make work pass or fail, but to say truthfully whether it meets the limits.

ul: Judge only against the written limits, and record the facts honestly, with measurements.
Never sign for work you did not see or check.

If a manager, welder or client presses you to pass work that does not meet the limits ("just this once"), record a non-conformance and refer it to the person the quality system names. Only an authorised person can accept non-conforming work, in writing.
Never change a drawing or tolerance yourself so that work passes.

blocks.h: What you need before you start

head: Document
Why
rows: Drawings (latest revision)
Sizes, weld sizes and types, materials, tolerances
Specification and the code it calls up
Acceptance limits for defects and dimensions; the tests required
Inspection and test plan (ITP)
What is inspected at each stage, by whom, by which method; hold and witness points
Weld map
The number of every weld, to link results, welders and procedures
Written test procedures
How each NDT method is to be done on this job
Previous reports and NCRs
Open problems and repairs to check

head: Stage
Checks
rows: Before welding
Documents approved; materials and heat numbers; consumables; welder qualifications; fit-up: root gap, bevel angle, root face, alignment, tack quality, cleanliness
During welding
Preheat and interpass temperature; settings against the WPS; cleaning between runs; back gouging; consumable control
After welding
Visual inspection of every weld; NDT as the ITP says; dimensions; repairs re-inspected; inspected and released **before painting**, because paint hides cracks and surface faults
Final
All tests passed or NCRs closed; records complete; release note issued

blocks.p: If you find a weld that was painted before anyone inspected it, do not pass it on the strength of the paint, and do not scrap the item either: remove the paint at that weld, inspect it, and record what you did.

blocks.note: On a full-penetration joint, the fit-up check that matters most is the **root gap and bevel**: if they are wrong, the root cannot fuse fully, and no amount of skill on the day will fix it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Checking the records behind the welds

flow: Start from the weld map: every weld, its welder and its WPS
For each WPS: approved, and backed by a PQR (or allowed as prequalified) whose ranges cover the joint, material, thickness, position and consumables
For each welder: the qualification covers the process, position and thickness of the welds he made, it is signed by the examiner, and the continuity record shows it was current on the dates
For materials: heat numbers on the steel match the mill certificates and the grade on the drawing
For consumables: certificates, oven and issue logs; preheat and NDT records where needed
Any gap (for example a weld by an unqualified welder) is raised as a non-conformance, and the weld is reviewed or retested

blocks.p: To witness a welder qualification test or a procedure test, you watch it **from start to finish**. If you arrive after the root has been run, you cannot confirm it was made to the WPS without help: ask for the test to be restarted in your presence.
**Visual inspection (VT)** is the first and most used test. Every weld gets it, before any other NDT, and many faults are found and fixed this way at almost no cost.

ul: Clean the weld: slag, spatter and paint removed.
Good light. Shine a torch at a **low angle across the surface**: the shadows show up undercut, overlap, ripples, pits and cracks.
Get your eye close (within about 600 mm) and look from more than one direction; a magnifier helps with fine cracks.
Look at the whole weld: both toes, the face, the start and stop, the root where it can be seen, and the parent metal beside it (arc strikes, spatter, gouges).

head: Gauge
What it measures
rows: Fillet gauge
Leg length and, on some, throat; whether the face is convex or concave
Multi-purpose (bridge cam) gauge
Undercut depth, cap height (excess weld metal), misalignment, fillet throat and leg, and bevel angle
Hi-lo gauge
Internal misalignment of pipe ends at fit-up
Feeler gauges
Small gaps, such as fit-up gaps and the gaps of tension-indicating washers
Steel rule, tape, square, protractor
Lengths, positions, squareness and angles

blocks.p: A fillet weld is specified by its **leg length** (or sometimes its throat). The **throat** is the shortest distance from the root to the face. On an equal-leg fillet with a flat face, the throat is about **0.7 × the leg**.

ul: On a **concave** fillet the legs can be full size while the throat is too thin, so check the throat as well.
On a **convex** fillet the throat is fine, but too much convexity wastes metal and can give a sharp notch at the toe.
Check that both legs are equal (unless the drawing says otherwise).

head: Sum
Worked example
rows: Minimum throat = 0.7 × leg
For a 10 mm fillet: 0.7 × 10 = **7 mm**. A concave weld with 10 mm legs but a 6.2 mm throat is undersize.

head: Check
How to judge
Worked example (limits for this job)
rows: Porosity
Add up the pore diameters in the stated length and compare with the limit; check any single-pore limit too
Limit: total 8 mm in any 100 mm. Pores of 2, 2.5, 1.5 and 3 mm = 9 mm: **reject**
Undercut
Measure the depth with the gauge; check its length if the limit allows short lengths
Limit 0.5 mm deep. Measured 0.4 mm: **accept**
Misalignment (step between plate faces)
Compare the step with the limit, often a percentage of the thickness
Limit 10% of 16 mm = 1.6 mm. Measured 1.2 mm: **accept**
Cap height (excess weld metal)
Measure height above the plate surface
Limit 3 mm. Measured 3.5 mm: **reject** (grind to limit)
Cracks
Most codes allow none
Any crack: **reject**

blocks.note: Write down the measured value, not just "OK". A report that says "undercut 0.4 mm, limit 0.5 mm, accept" can be checked by anyone; "looks fine" cannot.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Welding heat pulls steel out of shape, and marking or cutting errors put holes and parts in the wrong place. Dimensional inspection checks the finished item against the drawing and its tolerances, before it leaves the shop and before it is painted.

ul: Use tapes, rules and squares that are **in calibration** and undamaged (check the tape's hook and the square's blade).
Read the drawing and the tolerances for each dimension. Choose **datums**: the faces, edges or hole centres you measure from.
Set the item **level on firm supports**, so it does not sag or twist under its own weight, and chock it so it cannot roll or tip.

Measure in the cooler part of the day where you can. A beam heated by the sun on one side bends towards the cooler side for a while, and steel grows by about 0.012 mm per metre for each 1 °C (a 10 m beam 20 °C hotter is about 2.4 mm longer).

head: Fault
What it is
How to check
rows: Camber
An upward or downward bow along the length of a beam
Stretch a fine line between spacer blocks at each end of the top flange (or use a level), and measure the largest gap
Sweep
A sideways bow along the length, seen from above
The same method along the side of a flange
Twist
The ends turned in opposite directions about the long axis
Lay straight edges across each end and sight across them; they should be parallel
Flatness
Hollows or humps on a plate or end plate
A straight edge laid in several directions, with feeler gauges under it
Squareness
An end plate or frame corner not at 90°
A square; on a frame, measure both diagonals: equal diagonals mean square

head: Sum
Worked example
rows: Allowed bow when the limit is length ÷ 1 000
Shortest and longest that pass
Diagonal of a rectangle (Pythagoras)

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Pitch
The distance between hole centres along a line
Gauge
The distance between lines of holes, across the member
Edge distance
From a hole centre to the nearest edge of the plate
Hole size
Diameter, checked with a rule, caliper or gauge

ul: Measure hole positions from the stated datum, centre to centre, not edge to edge of the holes.
A hole outside its tolerance is recorded as a non-conformance. It is not "fixed" by flame-cutting the hole bigger or drilling a new hole next to it without the engineer's approval.

blocks.note: Every reading goes on the inspection sheet beside its tolerance and the result. Two people checking each other's readings, and settling any difference by measuring again, catches most measuring mistakes.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A bolted connection is only as good as its bolts, its holes and the way it was tightened. Check the drawing and specification for the bolt grade, size, length and tightening method before you start.

head: Check
What to look for
rows: Bolt, nut and washer grade
Markings on the bolt head and nut match the specification (for example property class 8.8 bolts with matching nuts). A lower-grade bolt (for example one marked 4.6) mixed in is replaced.
Size and length
Diameter and length as drawn. The bolt must stand **at least flush** with the outer face of the nut, and usually a thread or more past it.
Condition
Clean, undamaged threads; nuts run on freely; no rust or paint on threads where it matters
Holes
Right size and position; not torn or burred; not enlarged or slotted by flame cutting unless the drawing allows it
Plates
Pulled tight together with no gap beyond the limit; contact faces as specified (for example unpainted where friction grip is needed)
Washers
Under the part that is turned (usually the nut), the right way up; bevelled washers on sloping flanges
Tightness
Checked by the method the specification gives (below)

blocks.h: Tightening methods and how to check them

head: Method
How it is done
What the inspector checks
rows: Snug tight
Tightened with a normal spanner by one person, or a few impacts of an impact wrench, until the plates are pulled together
Plates in firm contact; no loose bolts
Part-turn (turn-of-nut)
Snug tight first, then a **match mark** is painted across nut, bolt end and plate, and the nut is turned a further set amount (for example a half turn)
The match marks show the nut has turned the required amount from snug
Torque control
A calibrated torque wrench to a set torque
Wrench in calibration; a sample of bolts checked
Direct tension indicators (tension-indicating washers)
Small bumps on the washer flatten as the bolt is tightened
Gaps between the bumps closed as far as the maker says, checked with a feeler gauge

blocks.note: Record each connection on the inspection sheet: its location, the bolt grade and size, stand-out, washers, the tightening check and the result. One loose or wrong bolt is a non-conformance, not a detail.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Surface NDT: dye penetrant and magnetic particle testing

blocks.p: Non-destructive testing (NDT) finds faults without damaging the part. **Dye penetrant (PT)** and **magnetic particle (MT)** testing find faults at or near the surface, which is where most fatigue cracks start. Both must be done by a trained person to a written procedure and the maker's instructions.

Red dye is drawn into surface-breaking defects by capillary action. After the excess is removed, a thin white **developer** draws the dye back out, so a defect shows as a red mark on white. PT works on any non-porous metal: carbon and stainless steel, aluminium, copper.

flow: Check the part is within the temperature range the maker gives (often about 10–50 °C) and read the SDS
Pre-clean: remove slag, spatter, paint and oil, then clean with the cleaner and let it **dry**: dirt or water in a crack keeps the dye out
Apply penetrant over the area and leave it for the **dwell time** the maker gives, keeping it wet
Remove the excess: wipe with a dry lint-free cloth, then with a cloth **damped** with cleaner. Never spray cleaner straight onto the weld: it washes dye out of the defects
Shake the developer and spray a **thin, even** coat from the distance the maker gives
Wait the development time, then inspect in good white light
Measure each indication, judge it against the limits and record it with a sketch
Post-clean the part; put used cloths in a closed metal bin

head: Indication
Usually means
rows: A sharp red line
A crack, lack of fusion at the surface, or a lap
Round red dots, alone or in groups
Porosity (pores open to the surface)
General pink background
Excess penetrant not properly removed, or a rough surface: clean and repeat

ul: **Developer too thick** (like paint) hides fine indications. Too thin, and the dye is not drawn out.
Grinding a weld with a coarse disc just before PT can **smear metal over the mouth of a crack**, so the dye cannot get in. Follow the procedure on surface preparation.
Every mark is an **indication** until it is judged: some are false (scratches, edges, poor cleaning).

blocks.p: A magnetic field is put into the part, often with a hand-held electromagnet called a **yoke** placed with its two legs either side of the area. Where a crack breaks the field, it leaks out at the surface and attracts fine iron particles in the magnetic ink, making a visible line. MT finds cracks **at or just below the surface**, but only in **magnetic (ferritic) steels**. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminium and copper are not magnetic, so they are tested with PT.

flow: Check the yoke: lead, plug and case undamaged and in electrical test; keep it away from water
Do a **lift test**: the yoke must lift the test weight the procedure gives (often about 4.5 kg for an AC yoke) at its working leg spacing, to prove it is strong enough
Clean the weld of slag and spatter; spray a thin coat of **white contrast paint** and let it dry, so black particles show clearly
Place the yoke legs across the weld, switch on, apply the ink while the field is on, let it drain, then switch off
Turn the yoke about **90°** and test the same area again
Move along the weld with the tested areas overlapping
Measure, judge and record each indication; clean off ink and paint; demagnetise if the specification asks

head: Yoke placed
Field runs
Shows best
rows: Legs either side of the weld (across it)
Across the weld
Cracks running **along** the weld, such as toe cracks
Legs along the weld line
Along the weld
Cracks running **across** the weld

blocks.note: A crack lying in the same direction as the field does not disturb it and will not show. That is why every area is tested twice, with the yoke turned about 90°.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: MT is quick on site and does not need the long dwell times of PT, but it cannot find deep buried faults such as porosity or lack of fusion in the middle of thick welds.
Some false indications appear at sharp changes of section, edges and scratches: judge them carefully.

sections.title: Ultrasonic and radiographic testing, and choosing a test

blocks.p: **Ultrasonic testing (UT)** and **radiographic testing (RT)** look inside the weld. They are done by qualified operators (and RT images are read by qualified interpreters) from specialist companies. The welding inspector must understand them well enough to choose the right test, prepare the welds, read the reports and act on the results.

ul: A hand-held **probe** sends high-frequency sound into the steel and picks up the echoes. A flaw reflects sound, and the screen shows where.
A gel or oil called **couplant** is spread between the probe and the steel, because sound will not cross an air gap.
The flaw detector is set up on a **calibration block** (a steel block with known holes or notches) before testing.
Angle probes send the sound in at an angle to reach the weld from the plate beside it.

UT is good at finding **planar** (flat) flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks, and gives their **depth** and length. It needs no radiation, so work nearby can go on. It suits thick butt welds and is often used on site.
Limits: it needs a skilled operator, and a basic UT test leaves no picture to keep unless the equipment records the scan. It is harder on thin, coarse-grained or oddly shaped parts.
A straight (0°) probe also finds **laminations** (flat layers) inside plate, for example before a tee joint is welded onto it.

X-rays or gamma rays pass through the weld onto a film or digital plate. Thinner or less dense places (pores, slag, lack of penetration) let more radiation through and show **darker**; denser things (tungsten) show **lighter**.

Each image must show an **image quality indicator (IQI)**: a set of fine wires or holes. If the required wire or hole cannot be seen, the image is not sharp or sensitive enough, and it cannot be used to accept the weld: it is retaken.
Markers on each image show the weld number and its location, so the image can be matched to the weld map.
RT gives a **lasting record** of the whole weld for the client's file.
Radiation is dangerous. The area is barriered and cleared, often at night or at breaks, and only licensed operators work inside it. Everyone else stays out, as the radiographers direct.

head: On the image
Usually means
rows: Round dark spots, scattered or in clusters
Porosity
Dark, uneven shapes or broken lines
Slag inclusions
A straight dark line along the centre of the root
Lack of root penetration
A dark line along the edge of the weld
Lack of side-wall fusion
Fine, dark, wavy lines
Cracks
Small bright white spots
Tungsten inclusions
A light band along the root
Excess penetration

blocks.p: If you are not a qualified interpreter, your part is to check that the report covers every weld on the weld map that needed RT, that the images are properly identified, to record the results and repairs, and to raise any query with the testing company.

head: Job
Best choice
Why
rows: Surface cracks in carbon steel fillet welds, on site
MT
Magnetic steel; quick; finds surface and near-surface cracks
Cracks in stainless steel or aluminium welds
PT
Not magnetic; PT works on any non-porous metal
Buried lack of fusion in a thick butt weld
UT
Finds planar flaws, gives their depth; no radiation barrier
A lasting record of a pipe butt weld
RT
A picture of the whole weld that can be kept
Laminations in plate before welding onto it
UT (straight probe)
Finds flat flaws inside plate
Every weld, first
VT
Cheap, fast, finds most surface faults

blocks.p: UT gives the depth of a flaw, so you can plan the repair from the nearer face. In 25 mm plate, a flaw found 18 mm below face A is only 7 mm below face B: excavating from face B removes far less sound metal.
Destructive tests cut or break a test piece to see inside the weld. They are used on welder and procedure qualification tests, on production test plates, and sometimes on a sample from a batch.

head: Test
How it is done
What it shows
rows: Macro section (macro-etch)
A slice is sawn across the weld away from the start and stop; the face is filed, then sanded with finer and finer paper until smooth, then etched with the approved etchant
The weld metal, the passes, the **fusion line** (where weld meets parent metal), the HAZ; root penetration and fusion, leg lengths and throat; cracks, pores, slag, lack of fusion between runs
Fillet break test
A length of fillet weld is broken by bending the upright plate over towards the weld, in a press or with a hammer, so the root opens
The fracture face: root fusion, porosity and slag inside the fillet
Nick-break test
Saw cuts are made into each side of a butt weld, then it is broken
The cuts make the break run through the weld metal, so its inside can be seen: fusion, pores, slag
Bend tests (face, root, side)
A strip across the weld is bent round a former
Ductility and soundness: open defects on the stretched surface, judged against the code's limit
Tensile test
A specimen is pulled until it breaks
Strength
Hardness test
A small indenter is pressed into the weld, HAZ and parent metal
Hardened zones that may crack

ul: Scratches left on a macro face hide the outline of the weld: finish to a fine paper before etching.
Etchants are chemicals: use gloves, goggles and ventilation as the SDS says.
Record results with photos and measurements, and keep the specimens labelled until the job is closed.

head: Result (limits for this job)
Judgement
rows: Root bend opens a 4 mm defect; limit 3 mm
Fail
Macro shows the weld did not reach the root corner
Incomplete root penetration: fail if the joint calls for full fusion to the root
Macro shows a dark, unfused line between two runs
Lack of inter-run fusion: fail
Fillet break face fully fused, two pores of 1 mm; limit 2 mm each
Pass

blocks.h: When an item does not conform

flow: Mark the item and tag or quarantine it so it cannot be used by mistake
Write a non-conformance report (NCR): the item, the requirement, what was found (measurements, sketch or photo), who found it and when
The authorised person decides the **disposition**
The action is carried out
The item is inspected again
The NCR is closed, and the cause is dealt with so it does not happen again

head: Disposition
Meaning
rows: Rework
Work it again so it fully meets the drawing (for example grind an oversize cap to the limit)
Repair
Make it fit for use by an approved repair procedure, which may not restore it exactly to the drawing
Use as is (concession)
Accept it as it is, with **written** approval from the customer or the engineer
Regrade
Use it for a different, less demanding purpose
Scrap
Reject it completely

blocks.note: The inspector does not grant a concession on his own. He records the facts and the decision of the person authorised to make it, and checks that it is in writing before the item is released.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Job, drawing number and revision, item and weld numbers from the weld map.
Material and process; the code or specification and the acceptance limits used.
Inspection method and stage; equipment with its serial or calibration number; conditions; date.
Measured results for each weld or dimension, not just "good" or "bad".
Each defect described by type and size, and its position shown on a **sketch with the weld number, a datum and the distance** from it; photos where useful.
Accept or reject against each limit; any NCR raised.
Signed and dated by the inspector, with their qualification; clear, legible, filed so it can be traced.

blocks.p: When everything has passed, an **inspection release note** (or certificate of conformity) records that the item met its requirements and may go on to the next stage or to the customer.

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Inspecting at height
Safe access (scaffold, platform, MEWP) and fall protection where needed; never climb the steel
Aerosol sprays (penetrant, cleaner, developer, contrast paint, ink)
Read the SDS; good ventilation; away from heat and flames; nitrile gloves and safety glasses
Used cloths
Into a closed metal bin, away from heat
Mains-powered yoke
Check lead, plug and case; keep away from water
Radiography
Stay outside the barrier; follow the radiographers
Heavy items
Lifting gear or enough people; chock items on supports
Hot work nearby
Eye protection from arcs; keep clear of sparks

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can explain why an inspector must stay independent and how to deal with pressure to pass work.
I can list the documents I need before an inspection, and the checks at each stage.
I can check from the records that welds were made by qualified welders to approved procedures with traceable materials.
I can carry out visual inspection and use fillet, bridge cam and hi-lo gauges.
I can work out a fillet throat and judge porosity, undercut, misalignment and cap height against limits.
I can measure camber, sweep, twist, flatness, squareness and hole positions from a datum.
I can inspect a bolted connection, including bolt grade, stand-out, washers and tightness.
I can carry out a colour-contrast dye penetrant test step by step.
I can carry out a magnetic particle test with a yoke, including the lift test and two directions.
I can explain how UT and RT work, read the meaning of common RT images, and say when each is used.
I can choose a suitable test for a job and explain why.
I can prepare and judge a macro section, fillet break, nick-break and bend test.
I can raise an NCR, explain the disposition choices and write a good inspection report.
I can work safely as an inspector.

terms: A steel block with known holes or notches used to set up a UT flaw detector
An upward or downward bow along the length of a beam
Written approval to use an item that does not fully meet its requirements
Gel or oil that lets sound pass from the UT probe into the steel
The thin white coating that draws dye out of defects in PT
The decision on what happens to a non-conforming item
How long the penetrant is left on before the excess is removed
From a hole centre to the nearest edge of the plate
The boundary between weld metal and parent metal
Any sign seen in NDT before it is judged to be a defect or not
Image quality indicator: shows a radiograph is sensitive enough
A check that an MT yoke can lift a set test weight
A polished and etched cross-section of a weld
A butt weld nicked with saw cuts and broken to show its inside
The hand-held part of a UT set that sends and receives sound
A record that an item passed inspection and may go on
A sideways bow along the length of a beam, seen from above
The shortest distance from the root of a fillet weld to its face
Ends of a member turned in opposite directions about its long axis
A hand-held two-legged electromagnet used for MT

c1.title: Conveyor frame welds at a quarry near Rio Bueno
c1.text: Tamika is inspecting the welds on a new carbon steel conveyor frame at a limestone quarry near Rio Bueno, Trelawny. The drawing calls for 8 mm fillet welds. The limits for this job are: undercut no deeper than 0.5 mm; no single pore over 2 mm; total pore diameters no more than 6 mm in any 100 mm of weld; fillet throat at least 0.7 × the specified leg. On one fillet she measures 8 mm legs but a concave face with a 4.9 mm throat. On another she finds undercut 0.8 mm deep for 30 mm along one toe. On a third, one 100 mm length has pores of 1, 1.5, 2 and 2 mm. She must also check the main fillets for toe cracks with an AC yoke.

c2.title: A stainless water tank for a clinic in Ulster Spring
c2.text: Devon is dye penetrant testing the welds of a grade 304 stainless steel water tank for a health clinic in Ulster Spring, Trelawny. The welder ground the welds smooth with a coarse disc just before the test. Devon sprays the developer on heavily until the welds look painted white. When the development time is up he sees a sharp red line about 12 mm long along one toe and, on another weld, a cluster of small round red dots.

c3.title: Column splices for a car park in New Kingston
c3.text: Kirk is the welding inspector for butt-welded column splices in 32 mm plate on a multi-storey car park in New Kingston. A testing company does UT and RT. The UT report gives a planar indication 40 mm long, 24 mm below face A of one splice. On another splice the radiograph's IQI does not show the wire the procedure calls for. Kirk is not qualified to interpret radiographs.

c4.title: Rafters for a school canteen in Gayle
c4.text: Natalie is inspecting four steel rafters, each 9.6 m long, for a school canteen in Gayle, St Mary, before they are painted. The specification allows camber and sweep of up to the length ÷ 1 000. One rafter has a sweep of 12 mm. The apex connections use M16 bolts of property class 8.8, tightened by the part-turn method. In one connection she finds a bolt head marked 4.6, and another bolt ends two threads short of the outer face of its nut.

c5.title: Tests and a concession at a shop in Mile Gully
c5.text: Shawn is the inspector at a fabrication shop in Mile Gully, Manchester. A welder's root bend specimen has opened a 4 mm defect; the code's limit for this test is 3 mm. An etched macro from another test plate shows a dark, unfused line between two runs. Separately, a batch of brackets has holes drilled 3 mm off position, and the customer's engineer has agreed in writing to accept them as they are.

questions.q: What is the result for the concave fillet with 8 mm legs and a 4.9 mm throat?
o: Accept: both legs are the full 8 mm the drawing asks for
Accept: a concave face is always stronger than a flat one
Reject: the throat is under the 5.6 mm minimum
Reject: concave fillets are never allowed by any code
questions.why: The minimum throat is 0.7 × 8 = 5.6 mm. A concave face can leave the throat thin even when the legs are full size, which is why the inspector measures both.

questions.q: How should Tamika record the undercut?
o: Accept it, as it is less than 1 mm deep at its worst point
Reject it: 0.8 mm deep over 30 mm, beyond the 0.5 mm limit
Accept it, because it runs along only 30 mm of the weld
Leave it off the report and ask the welder to grind it
questions.why: Undercut deeper than the limit is a reject, and the report gives the measured depth, its length and position. Its repair is then done to procedure and re-inspected.

questions.q: How should Tamika judge the third fillet?
o: Accept: no single pore is larger than the 2 mm limit
Accept: 6.5 mm rounds down to the 6 mm total allowed
Reject: any porosity at all fails a structural weld
Reject: the total of 6.5 mm is over the 6 mm limit
questions.why: Both limits apply. Each pore is within 2 mm, but the total, 1 + 1.5 + 2 + 2 = 6.5 mm, is over the 6 mm allowed in 100 mm, so the length fails.

questions.q: To look for cracks running along the toes, how should Tamika place the yoke first?
o: Legs along the weld line, so the field runs with the weld
Legs either side of the weld, so the field crosses it
One leg on the weld face and one on the base plate
Anywhere on the frame, since the field spreads through it
questions.why: A crack shows best when it lies across the field. With the legs either side of the weld, the field runs across it and toe cracks along the weld break it. She then turns the yoke about 90° to find cracks running the other way.

questions.q: What is wrong with how Devon applied the developer?
o: Nothing: a thick coat makes small indications easier to see
He should have brushed it on rather than sprayed it
Too thick a coat can hide fine indications
Developer must be applied before the penetrant
questions.why: Developer should be a thin, even coat from the distance the maker gives. A thick layer covers fine cracks so the dye cannot show through, and the test may need to be repeated.

questions.q: Why might grinding with a coarse disc just before the test hide cracks?
o: The disc leaves a shiny surface that reflects the light
Grinding can smear metal over the mouth of a crack
The heat from grinding makes the dye dry out too fast
Ground stainless steel will no longer take up the dye
questions.why: Grinding can spread a thin layer of metal over a crack opening, so the penetrant cannot get in and the crack shows nothing. The test procedure sets how the surface is prepared, and some need a light etch first.

questions.q: How should Devon treat the 12 mm red line along the toe?
o: As a linear indication, likely a crack: measure, record, judge
As porosity, since dye always spreads out from the pores
As left-over dye from poor cleaning: wipe it and pass the weld
As normal for stainless steel, which always shows some lines
questions.why: A sharp red line usually means a crack or lack of fusion at the surface, while round dots usually mean porosity. Each indication is measured, sketched and judged against the limits; most codes allow no cracks.

questions.q: From which face should the flaw 24 mm below face A be dug out?
o: Face A, because the report measures from that face
Face B, where it is only about 8 mm below the surface
Both faces at once, meeting in the middle of the plate
Neither: planar flaws in UT are always left in place
questions.why: In 32 mm plate, a flaw 24 mm below face A is 32 − 24 = 8 mm below face B. Excavating from the nearer face removes far less sound metal and gives a smaller repair.

questions.q: What does it mean that the IQI wire does not show on the radiograph?
o: The weld is free of all defects, so there is nothing to show
The IQI was placed upside down, but the image can be read
The weld is too thick to radiograph and must use PT
The image is not sensitive enough, so it must be retaken
questions.why: The IQI proves the image can show small flaws. If the required wire or hole is not visible, the radiograph cannot be used to accept the weld; it is retaken with corrected settings.

questions.q: What is Kirk's part in dealing with the RT results?
o: Read the films himself and overrule the testing company
Sign the RT report so the interpreter does not need to
Check RT covers every weld it should; record and query
Accept any weld whose film he cannot read clearly
questions.why: Radiographs are read and signed by a qualified interpreter. The welding inspector checks the report against the weld map, makes sure each image is identified, records results and repairs, and raises queries with the testing company.

questions.q: What is the result for the rafter with 12 mm of sweep?
o: Accept: the limit is 96 mm for a 9.6 m rafter
Accept: only camber matters on a roof rafter
Reject: the limit is 9.6 mm, so raise an NCR
Accept: 12 mm is less than 1% of the length
questions.why: Length ÷ 1 000 = 9 600 ÷ 1 000 = 9.6 mm. A sweep of 12 mm is over the limit, so it is recorded as a non-conformance with the measurements and a sketch. The disposition (for example flame straightening) is decided by the authorised person.

questions.q: What should Natalie do about the bolt marked 4.6?
o: Accept it, since it is the right diameter and fully tight
Have it replaced with a class 8.8 bolt and record it
Paint it a different colour so it can be watched
Tighten it further so it reaches the 8.8 strength
questions.why: Head markings show the bolt's grade. A class 4.6 bolt is much weaker than the 8.8 specified, and no amount of tightening changes that. It is replaced with the right grade, and the finding goes on the inspection sheet.

questions.q: What about the bolt that ends two threads short of the nut face?
o: Accept it, as long as the nut is fully tightened
Accept it if the washer is removed to gain thread
Accept it if a second nut is added behind the first
Reject it: fit a bolt long enough to pass the nut
questions.why: The bolt must stand at least flush with the outer face of the nut, usually a thread or more past it, so every thread of the nut is engaged. A short bolt is replaced; removing the specified washer is not allowed.

questions.q: How should Natalie check that the part-turn bolts were tightened correctly?
o: Check that the match marks show the set amount of turn
Hit each nut with a hammer and listen for a ringing sound
Try to turn each nut further with a short spanner by hand
Ask the erector how many turns he gave each of the nuts
questions.why: In the part-turn method each bolt is made snug, a match mark is painted across nut, bolt and plate, and the nut is then turned a set amount. The marks show the inspector how far each nut has turned.

questions.q: What is the result of the root bend test?
o: Pass: some opening is normal in any bend test
Pass, if the face bend from the same plate is good
Fail: the 4 mm defect is over the 3 mm limit
Retest the same strip by bending it a second time
questions.why: A defect that opens beyond the code's limit on the stretched face fails the specimen. The welder has not passed; any retest follows the code's rules, with new test pieces.

questions.q: What does the dark, unfused line between two runs on the macro show?
o: Lack of inter-run fusion
Normal fusion line between runs
Incomplete root penetration
Excess weld metal on the cap
questions.why: Each run should fuse into the one below. A dark line between runs on an etched macro means they did not fuse, often from too little heat, poor cleaning or a wrong angle, and the test plate fails.

questions.q: How should Shawn deal with the brackets the engineer has accepted?
o: Pass them with no paperwork, since the engineer has agreed
Reject them anyway, as the inspector's decision is final
Re-drill the holes in the right place before releasing them
Record the concession on the NCR, then close it and release
questions.why: This disposition is "use as is" under a written concession from the authorised person. The inspector records it on the NCR with the reference to the engineer's approval, closes the NCR, and then releases the brackets.

questions.q: Why is it better to measure the length and sweep of a long beam early in the morning than in the afternoon sun?
o: Steel tapes stretch when they get hot in the sun
Sun on one side bends the beam and makes it grow
The paint is softer and easier to mark early on
It is easier to read the tape in the morning light
questions.why: Steel grows about 0.012 mm per metre for each 1 °C. When the sun heats one side, that side grows and the beam bends towards the cool side, so readings are wrong until it evens out.

questions.q: A thick plate will have a tee joint welded onto its face. Which test would find laminations inside the plate first?
o: Dye penetrant on the surface
Magnetic particle with a yoke
Ultrasonic with a straight probe
A fillet break test on the plate
questions.why: Laminations are flat layers inside the plate, parallel to its surface. A straight (0°) ultrasonic probe sends sound straight down and finds them. Surface methods cannot see inside the plate.

questions.q: An inspector finds that the next run has already been welded over a joint at a hold point he had not released. What should he do?
o: Release it now, since the work has already been done
Pass it if the welder says the joint looked good
Ask the welder to grind the top run off and say nothing
Raise an NCR and refer it for a decision on the joint
questions.why: Work passed a hold point without release, so the stage that should have been inspected is now hidden. He records a non-conformance and refers it; the decision may be extra NDT or removing the covering run.
